claim: The histone chaperone chromatin assembly factor 1 (CAF-1) deposits two nascent histone H3/H4 dimers onto newly replicated DNA forming the central core of the nucleosome known as the tetrasome.
source: The histone chaperone chromatin assembly factor 1 (CAF-1) deposits two nascent histone H3/H4 dimers onto newly replicated DNA forming the central core of the nucleosome known as the tetrasome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction to prior work (Smith and Stillman, 1989; Kaufman et al., 1995; Mattiroli et al., 2017; Sauer et al., 2017; Sauer et al., 2018).

claim: The KER region of CAF-1 is a 128-Å single alpha-helix (SAH) motif.
source: Structural and biophysical characterization of the lysine/glutamic acid/arginine-rich (KER) region of CAF-1 revealed a 128-Å single alpha-helix (SAH) motif with unprecedented DNA-binding properties.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural data presented in Figure 2a showing the crystal structure with a 128 Å helix.

claim: The KER SAH has unprecedented DNA-binding properties.
source: Structural and biophysical characterization of the lysine/glutamic acid/arginine-rich (KER) region of CAF-1 revealed a 128-Å single alpha-helix (SAH) motif with unprecedented DNA-binding properties.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by EMSA data in Figures 1 and 4 showing DNA binding of the KER domain.

claim: The KER SAH drives the selectivity of CAF-1 for tetrasome-length DNA.
source: Distinct KER sequence features and length of the SAH drive the selectivity of CAF-1 for tetrasome-length DNA and facilitate function in budding yeast.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by DNA ladder EMSA experiments in Figure 4 showing preferential binding to 40-50 bp DNA.

claim: The KER cooperates with the DNA-binding winged helix domain in CAF-1 to overcome DNA damage sensitivity in vivo.
source: In vivo, the KER cooperates with the DNA-binding winged helix domain in CAF-1 to overcome DNA damage sensitivity and maintain silencing of gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by yeast spot assays in Figure 1n showing that deletion of both KER and WHD results in high sensitivity to DNA damaging agents.

claim: The KER cooperates with the winged helix domain in CAF-1 to maintain silencing of gene expression in vivo.
source: In vivo, the KER cooperates with the DNA-binding winged helix domain in CAF-1 to overcome DNA damage sensitivity and maintain silencing of gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by GFP silencing assays in Figure 1o showing loss of silencing when both KER and WHD are disrupted.

claim: The KER SAH acts as a DNA-binding spacer element during chromatin assembly.
source: We propose that the KER SAH links functional domains within CAF-1 with structural precision, acting as a DNA-binding spacer element during chromatin assembly.
evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the abstract and discussed in the Discussion section, based on the structural and functional data presented.

claim: The nucleosome comprises two H3/H4 and two H2A/H2B histone dimers wrapped by approximately 147 bp of DNA.
source: The nucleosome is the fundamental unit of chromatin, comprising two H3/H4 and two H2A/H2B histone dimers wrapped by approximately 147 bp of DNA (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Luger et al., 1997.

claim: DNA replication requires the disassembly of parental nucleosomes followed by a highly regulated dynamic assembly process for recycling of parental histones and depositing nascent histones onto newly replicated DNA.
source: DNA replication requires the disassembly of parental nucleosomes, followed by a highly regulated dynamic assembly process for recycling of parental histones and depositing nascent histones onto the newly replicated DNA (Smith and Stillman, 1991; Escobar et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Smith and Stillman, 1991 and Escobar et al., 2021.

claim: CAF-1 facilitates the dimerization of nascent H3/H4 dimers onto replicated DNA, forming the subnucleosomal structure known as the tetrasome.
source: The histone chaperone chromatin assembly factor 1 (CAF-1) facilitates the dimerization of nascent H3/H4 dimers onto replicated DNA, forming the subnucleosomal structure known as the tetrasome (Smith and Stillman, 1989; Kaufman et al., 1995; Mattiroli et al., 2017; Sauer et al., 2017; Sauer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: The essential functions of CAF-1 are required for the maintenance of epigenetic landscapes and gene expression patterns in multicellular organisms.
source: In multicellular organisms, the essential functions of CAF-1 are required for the maintenance of epigenetic landscapes and gene expression patterns (Cheloufi et al., 2015; Cheloufi and Hochedlinger, 2017; Smith and Whitehouse, 2012; Ramachandran and Henikoff, 2016; Sauer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: Three subunits, Cac1, Cac2, and Cac3, form the CAF-1 complex.
source: Three subunits, Cac1, Cac2, and Cac3, form the CAF-1 complex (Sauer et al., 2018; Smith and Stillman, 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Interactions with the replisome through PCNA interacting peptides (PIP box) in the Cac1 subunit are central to the localization of CAF-1 to replicated DNA.
source: Central to the localization of CAF-1 to replicated DNA are interactions with the replisome through PCNA interacting peptides (PIP box) in the Cac1 subunit (Shibahara and Stillman, 1999; Krawitz et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The DNA-binding function of the winged helix domain (WHD) located in Cac1 contributes to the recruitment of CAF-1 to sites of replication.
source: Additionally, the DNA-binding function of the winged helix domain (WHD) located in Cac1 contributes to the recruitment of CAF-1 to sites of replication (Sauer et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016; Mattiroli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae CAF-1 (yCAF-1) has a preference for binding to DNA that is at least 40 bp long.
source: DNA-binding studies of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae CAF-1 (yCAF-1) revealed a preference for binding to DNA that is at least 40 bp long (Sauer et al., 2017), which is slightly less than the length of DNA needed to form a tetrasome (Luger et al., 1997; Donham et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The WHD binds to short (10–16 bp) DNA fragments.
source: As the WHD binds to short (10–16 bp) DNA fragments (Zhang et al., 2016; Mattiroli et al., 2017), it is unlikely to confer this DNA-length dependence to CAF-1 or allow for sufficient spacing for the assembly of tetrasomes in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The KER region of the Cac1 subunit has been implicated as a possible second DNA-binding domain because CAF-1 lacking the WHD could still bind to DNA.
source: However, the lysine/glutamic acid/arginine-rich (KER) region of the Cac1 subunit has been implicated as a possible second DNA-binding domain (DBD), as CAF-1 lacking the WHD could still bind to DNA (Sauer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation.

claim: yCAF-1 and the isolated KER and WHD domains bind to DNA with the appearance of a ladder of bands in EMSA, indicating that multiple proteins bind to a single DNA fragment.
source: yCAF-1 and the isolated domains bound to DNA with the appearance of a ladder of bands, especially for the yKER that has the largest number of bands, which are related to the length of the DNA fragment (20, 30, 40, and 80 bp). These results indicate that multiple proteins bind to a single DNA fragment (Figure 1f–i) and the Hill coefficients suggest a cooperative mode of DNA binding (Figure 1l).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by EMSA images in Figure 1f-i.

claim: The yKER has KD values between 18 and 50 nM for DNA of various lengths.
source: For DNA of the same length (Figure 1l), the yKER had KD values between 18 and 50 nM, whereas the yWHD bound three to six times more weakly.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1l.

claim: The yWHD binds DNA three to six times more weakly than the yKER.
source: For DNA of the same length (Figure 1l), the yKER had KD values between 18 and 50 nM, whereas the yWHD bound three to six times more weakly.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1l.

claim: yCAF-1 has a higher affinity for DNA fragments in the range of 50–80 bp, which are DNA lengths considered to be sufficient for tetrasome formation.
source: This analysis shows that yCAF-1 has a higher affinity for DNA fragments in the range of 50–80 bp, which are DNA lengths considered to be sufficient for tetrasome formation (Donham et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Donham et al., 2011 and supported by data in Figure 1l.

claim: Deletion of the KER region impairs DNA binding of yCAF-1.
source: Deletion of the KER region impaired DNA binding of yCAF-1 and also resulted in the failure of the complexes to migrate into the gel, possibly due to aggregation (Figure 1m).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1m.

claim: The KER binds more tightly to DNA than the WHD.
source: Together, these data show that the KER binds more tightly to DNA than the WHD and the presence of the KER in the context of yCAF-1 is needed for high DNA-binding affinity.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by KD values in Figure 1l.

claim: Yeast cells harboring defective CAF-1, including loss of the Cac1 subunit, or loss of its WHD, PIP box, or histone-binding regions, are more sensitive to DNA damaging agents.
source: Yeast cells harboring defective CAF-1, including loss of the Cac1 subunit, or loss of its WHD, PIP box, or histone-binding regions (Figure 1a), have been shown to be more sensitive to DNA damaging agents and have impaired establishment of chromatin landscapes (Li et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations.

claim: Deletion of Cac1 residues 136–225 (∆KER) results in mild sensitivity to CPT and Zeocin.
source: Deletion of Cac1 residues 136–225 that encode for the KER region (∆KER) resulted in a mild sensitivity to CPT and Zeocin (Figure 1n and Figure 1—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1n.

claim: Inhibition of the DNA-binding function of the WHD through point mutations in Cac1 residues K564E/K568E (mWHD) shows higher sensitivity to CPT and Zeocin than the deletion of the KER.
source: Inhibition of the DNA-binding function of the WHD through point mutations in Cac1 residues K564E/K568E (mWHD) in yeast (Zhang et al., 2016) showed higher sensitivity to CPT and Zeocin than the deletion of the KER.
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation and supported by data in Figure 1n.

claim: The double mutant ∆KER+mWHD shows higher CPT and Zeocin sensitivity than either mutant alone, and to a similar extent observed when the Cac1 subunit is absent (cac1∆).
source: Strikingly, the double mutant ∆KER+mWHD showed higher CPT and Zeocin sensitivity than either mutant alone, and to a similar extent observed when the Cac1 subunit is absent (cac1∆) (Figure 1n, Table 1, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1n and Table 1.

claim: At least one DNA-binding domain (KER or WHD) appears to be sufficient to maintain some CAF-1 function in vivo and overcome repercussions of DSBs.
source: These results are consistent with roles for both the KER and WHD in CAF-1 function because at least one DBD appears to be sufficient to maintain some CAF-1 function in vivo and overcome repercussions of DSBs, both dependent and independent of DNA replication.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the data from Figure 1n.

claim: The crystal structure of the KER was determined at 2.81 Å resolution.
source: Crystals grown of a maltose-binding protein (MBP)–KER fusion construct (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b, and Supplementary file 4) contained four copies of the MBP-yKER per asymmetric unit.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and the resolution is mentioned in the methods and Supplementary file 4.

claim: The yKER extends from the MBP as an almost entirely solvent exposed continuous alpha-helix.
source: The yKER extended from the MBP as an almost entirely solvent exposed continuous alpha-helix (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The longest yKER helix modeled is 128 Å long with 23 helical turns, encompassing Cac1 amino acids 136–221.
source: The longest yKER helix modeled (PDB 8DEI; molecule A) is 128 Å long with 23 helical turns, encompassing Cac1 amino acids 136–221 (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The yKER structure shows no evidence of interactions between yKER helices or formation of any tertiary structure, consistent with the definition of an SAH domain.
source: In the structure, we saw no evidence of interactions between yKER helices or formation of any tertiary structure, consistent with the definition of an SAH domain (Wolny et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Wolny et al., 2017.

claim: The yKER sequence reveals a pattern of opposite-charged residues, lysine/arginine and glutamic acid, that are three or four residues apart, capable of forming an ion pair network.
source: Inspection of the sequence of the yKER reveals a pattern of opposite-charged residues, lysine/arginine and glutamic acid, that are three or four residues apart (Figure 2b), capable of forming an ion pair network.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: An ion pair network confers stability to the helix so that SAH domains can be completely solvent exposed in solution.
source: Such a network confers stability to the helix so that SAH domains can be completely solvent exposed in solution (Batchelor et al., 2019; Sivaramakrishnan et al., 2008; Wolny et al., 2017; Swanson and Sivaramakrishnan, 2014); such as in the well-characterized Myosin 7a SAH (Barnes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results with multiple citations.

claim: The circular dichroism (CD) spectrum of the KER shows characteristics of only alpha helical secondary structure.
source: The circular dichroism (CD) spectrum of the KER showed characteristics of only alpha helical secondary structure, including the positive absorption band at 195 nm and two negative bands at 208 and 222 nm (Figure 2c), validating in solution the structure of the KER observed in the crystal.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Binding to DNA increases the alpha helical content of the yKER.
source: Interestingly, binding to DNA increased the alpha helical content of the yKER (Figure 2c) without changes in the CD signal from the DNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), suggesting that no major DNA structural changes occur.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2c.

claim: SAH domains exhibit non-cooperative denaturation transitions due to a lack of tertiary structure.
source: Fundamental to the definition of SAH domains is that they exhibit non-cooperative denaturation transitions due to a lack of tertiary structure (Wolny et al., 2017; Wolny et al., 2014; Süveges et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations.

claim: The thermal denaturation of the yKER exhibits non-cooperative behavior.
source: This behavior is also observed in the thermal denaturation monitored by CD at 222 nm of the yKER (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Chemical crosslinking with disuccinimidyl suberate (DSS) shows no evidence of KER multimers.
source: Furthermore, chemical crosslinking with disuccinimidyl suberate (DSS) showed no evidence of KER multimers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d), supporting the conclusion that the yKER does not form a tertiary structure.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: In the presence of 40 bp DNA, the thermal denaturation of the yKER shows an increase of 10°C in the melting temperature and a two-state cooperative unfolding transition.
source: In contrast, in the presence of 40 bp DNA, the thermal denaturation of the yKER showed an increase of 10°C in the melting temperature and a two-state cooperative unfolding transition (Figure 2d), which demonstrates the ability of the yKER to form a stably folded protein–DNA complex.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The monomeric state of the yKER suggests that the additional yKER–DNA complexes observed in the EMSAs are due to the addition of yKER monomers to the same molecule of DNA.
source: The monomeric state of the yKER also suggests that the additional yKER–DNA complexes observed in the EMSAs (Figure 1f–i) are due to the addition of yKER monomers to the same molecule of DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on inference from the crosslinking and EMSA data.

claim: Mixed-protein subunit:DNA complexes in heterogenous subunit EMSA can only be explained if the KER forms no obligate oligomers on the DNA.
source: The mixed-protein subunit:DNA complexes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e) can only be explained if the KER forms no obligate oligomers on the DNA. Rather, multiple monomers of yKER are recruited to the same molecule of DNA, creating the multiplicity of bands in the EMSA.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e.

claim: DNA binding has not been reported for other SAH domains even though they have a similar amino acid composition.
source: Finally, DNA binding has not been reported for other SAH domains even though they have a similar amino acid composition (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2c, d).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figures showing sequence comparisons.

claim: A purified Myosin 7a SAH shows no DNA binding in EMSA.
source: Examination of a purified Myosin 7a SAH (Barnes et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplement 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b) using EMSA detected no DNA binding, indicating that the DNA-binding properties of the yKER are not a general feature of SAH domains.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The yKER SAH is particularly enriched in positively charged residues, unlike the Myosin 7a SAH.
source: We noticed that the yKER SAH is particularly enriched in positively charged residues, unlike the Myosin 7a SAH (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c, d).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c, d.

claim: Positively charged residues in the yKER are biased toward one face of the helix and confer a net positive charge along most of the length of the yKER, concentrated toward the N-terminal and middle regions.
source: These residues are biased toward one face of the yKER helix and confer a net positive charge along most of the length of the yKER, which is concentrated toward the N-terminal and middle regions (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Only the middle-A protein (residues 155–204) exhibits strong DNA binding similar to the intact KER.
source: However, only the middle-A protein (residues 155–204) exhibited strong DNA binding similar to the intact KER (Figure 3a, c–g), whereas the N-half and middle-B constructs, which partially overlap with middle-A, did not bind well to DNA (Figure 3e, g).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3c-g.

claim: The middle-A region is required for DNA binding due to both the positively charged residues and alpha helical structure.
source: Although regions of the yKER outside of the middle-A region likely contribute to KER function, the middle-A region is required for DNA binding due to both the positively charged residues and alpha helical structure.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the truncation analysis in Figure 3.

claim: Deletion of the middle-A residues from yCAF-1 (yCAF1 ∆middle-A) abrogates binding of yCAF-1 to DNA.
source: Notably, deletion of the middle-A residues from yCAF-1 (yCAF1 ∆middle-A) abrogates binding of yCAF-1 to DNA (Figure 3h and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), confirming the importance of this region.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3h.

claim: yCAF1 ∆middle-A binds to DNA worse than the deletion of the KER (yCAF1 ∆KER).
source: Interestingly, we also observed that yCAF1 ∆middle-A binds to DNA worse than the deletion of the KER (yCAF1 ∆KER) (Figure 3h), suggesting that residual SAH structure might not support the correct organization or architecture of yCAF-1 in a manner that hinders the activity of the WHD.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3h.

claim: Substitution of the KER for the Myosin 7a SAH (KER::Myo7a) in yCAF-1 abolishes DNA binding.
source: In the context of CAF-1, a substitution of the KER for the Myosin 7a SAH (KER::Myo7a) in yCAF-1, also abolished DNA binding (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3h.

claim: ∆middle-A yeast behave like the ∆KER cells, exhibiting similar sensitivity to CPT and Zeocin.
source: In vivo, ∆middle-A yeast behave like the ∆KER cells, exhibiting similar sensitivity to CPT and Zeocin, and even higher GFP expression levels in the silencing assay when in combination with mWHD (Figure 3i, j, Table 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3i, j.

claim: A specific region within the KER domain (middle-A) simultaneously forms an alpha-helix and engages with DNA to drive DNA binding and the biological functions of yCAF-1.
source: Taken together, we conclude that a specific region within the KER domain (middle-A) simultaneously forms an alpha-helix and engages with DNA to drive DNA binding and the biological functions of yCAF-1.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the data in Figure 3.

claim: The KER, but not the WHD, equips yCAF-1 with a DNA-length selectivity function that favors binding to DNA fragments that are at least 40 bp in length.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that the KER, but not the WHD, equips yCAF-1 with a DNA-length selectivity function that favors binding to DNA fragments that are at least 40 bp in length.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the Cy5-DNA ladder assays in Figure 4.

claim: The presence of the WHD permits yCAF1 binding to 20 and 30 bp DNA.
source: Also, the presence of the WHD permits yCAF1 binding to 20 and 30 bp DNA, suggesting it has either a direct or indirect contribution to DNA binding of yCAF-1; and that there is a further contribution to the length threshold in the state where the WHD is released from the ED.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on comparison of yCAF-1 and yKER binding in Figure 4.

claim: yCAF-1 with an additional KER (yCAF1 2xKER) does not alter the DNA-length threshold of 40 bp.
source: Examination of yCAF1 2xKER in our Cy5-DNA ladder experiment showed that unexpectedly the additional KER did not alter the DNA-length threshold of 40 bp (Figure 4f, g and Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5a.

claim: yCAF1 2xKER (2xKER) exhibits mild sensitivity to CPT and Zeocin to a similar extent as seen for ∆KER cells.
source: In vivo, yCAF1 2xKER (2xKER) exhibited mild sensitivity to CPT (Figure 5b) and Zeocin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b) to a similar extent as seen for ∆KER cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5b.

claim: 2xKER in combination with inhibition of the WHD (2xKER+mWHD) does not have an additive effect unlike ∆KER in both CPT and Zeocin conditions.
source: Surprisingly, 2xKER in combination with inhibition of the WHD (2xKER+mWHD) did not have an additive effect unlike ∆KER in both CPT and Zeocin conditions (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The 2xKER mutant causes no significant loss of silencing in yeast and does not increase this effect when in combination with mWHD.
source: Likewise, the 2xKER mutant caused no significant loss of silencing in yeast and it did not increase this effect when in combination with mWHD (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5c.

claim: ∆145–149 cells behave like ∆KER cells, exhibiting similar sensitivity to CPT and Zeocin, as well as high GFP expression levels in the silencing assay when in combination with mWHD.
source: Interestingly, ∆145–149 cells behave like ∆KER cells, exhibiting similar sensitivity to CPT and Zeocin, as well as high GFP expression levels in our silencing assay when in combination with mWHD (Figure 5c, d, Table 1, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5c, d.

claim: Deletion of only the last two C terminal residues 225–226 (∆225–226) of the KER region produces identical results to ∆145–149.
source: Strikingly, identical results were found when only the deletion of the last two C terminal residues 225–226 (∆225–226) of the KER region in the Cac1 subunit were made (Figure 5e, c, Table 1, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b, c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5e, c.

claim: A very specific length and/or orientation of the yKER helix within CAF-1 is critical to overcome DNA damage and maintain gene silencing in vivo.
source: We conclude that a very specific length and/or orientation of the yKER helix within CAF-1 is critical to overcome DNA damage and maintain gene silencing in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the data in Figure 5.

claim: The human KER (hKER) has high alpha helical content and exhibits non-cooperative unfolding as expected for an SAH.
source: To address the hypothesis that the longer hKER might have different DNA-binding properties than the yKER, we expressed and purified the hKER (CHAF1A residues 331–441) and using CD found that it has high alpha helical content, and exhibits non-cooperative unfolding as expected for an SAH (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b, c.

claim: The hKER has identical DNA-length selectivity behavior to the yKER.
source: Subjecting the hKER to our Cy5-DNA ladder assay resulted in identical DNA-length selectivity behavior to the yKER (Figure 6b compared to 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Substitution of the yKER for the hKER in yCAF-1 (yCAF1 KER::hKER) slightly alters the DNA-length selectivity function of yCAF-1.
source: However, substitution of the yKER for the hKER in yCAF-1(yCAF1 KER::hKER) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a) slightly altered the DNA-length selectivity function of yCAF-1, as seen by the slight difference between the depletion of the 50 bp DNA fragments relative to the shorter DNA in our Cy5-DNA ladder assay (Figure 6c compared to Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The longer hKER can alter the DNA-length preference of yCAF-1.
source: This difference is largely due to the decreased competitiveness of the 30 and 40 bp DNA compared to the 50 bp DNA (Figure 4f, g). This is only observed in the context of yCAF-1 but not in the isolated KERs (Figure 4h) and suggests that the longer hKER can alter the DNA-length preference of yCAF-1.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on data in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Substitution of the KER for the hKER in yeast has a similar effect as the deletion of the KER, with similar sensitivity to CPT and Zeocin, as well as impaired chromatin silencing when in combination with mWHD.
source: Surprisingly, substitution of the KER for the hKER in yeast had a similar effect as the deletion of the KER, with similar sensitivity to CPT and Zeocin, as well as impaired chromatin silencing when in combination with mWHD (Figure 6d, e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6d, e.

claim: The hKER cannot substitute the yeast KER in vivo.
source: These results indicate that the hKER cannot substitute the yeast KER in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the data in Figure 6.

claim: The length of the KER alters the DNA-length selectivity and plays a critical role in CAF-1 biological functions.
source: Collectively, these results confirm the expected conservation of the overall SAH and DNA-binding characteristics of the KER from different species. Furthermore, and in agreement with our results in Figure 5, the length of the KER alters the DNA-length selectivity and plays a critical role in CAF-1 biological functions.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The KER is a first-in-class DBD, namely the 'SAH-DBD'.
source: It binds DNA in a non-sequence-specific manner with a binding affinity in the nM range, establishing it as a first-in-class DBD, namely the 'SAH-DBD'.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the structural and functional data presented.

claim: The KER is largely responsible for the observed DNA-length preference of CAF-1 for tetrasome-length DNA.
source: Moreover, we found that in the context of yCAF-1, the KER is largely responsible for observed DNA-length preference of CAF-1 for tetrasome-length DNA (Sauer et al., 2017) and CAF-1 function in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation and based on the data presented.

claim: The KER SAH is the longest SAH described to date (Cac1 aa 136–226; 90 aa).
source: The KER SAH is the longest SAH described to date (Cac1 aa 136–226; 90 aa) with the same general pattern of alternating basic and acidic amino acid residues as classic SAHs (Figure 2; Sivaramakrishnan et al., 2008; Batchelor et al., 2019; Dudola et al., 2017; Gáspári et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: The KER has a stripe of basic residues along most of the helix, so far only noticeable in the KER SAH of CAF-1.
source: However, the KER also has a stripe of basic residues along most of the helix, so far only noticeable in the KER SAH of CAF-1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on structural analysis.

claim: The KER of CAF-1 is the first SAH-DBD of its type within the larger group IV of 'other alpha-helix DNA-binding domains'.
source: The KER of CAF-1 is the first SAH-DBD of its type within the larger group IV of 'other alpha-helix DNA-binding domains' (Luscombe et al., 2000).Thus, the discovery that the KER is a DNA-binding SAH expands the repertoire of DBDs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation.

claim: The molecular mechanism of KER-DNA recognition requires both key positively charged residues and alpha helical conformation in the Cac1 middle-A section.
source: The molecular mechanism of KER-DNA recognition requires both key positively charged residues and alpha helical conformation in the Cac1 middle-A section (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data in Figure 3.

claim: The KER SAH is capable of binding to DNA independently and cooperatively in a final ratio related to the DNA length with an estimated site size as short as 20 bp.
source: Although CAF-1 prefers to bind to tetrasome-length DNA (Luger et al., 1997; Donham et al., 2011), the KER SAH is capable of binding to DNA independently and cooperatively in a final ratio related to the DNA length with an estimated site size as short as 20 bp, which is typical of many DBDs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations and based on EMSA data.

claim: The ability of CAF-1 to preferentially bind to a tetrasome length of DNA could ensure sufficient DNA is available so that as histone binding releases the WHD, there will be sufficient space along the DNA for the subsequent assembly of tetrasomes.
source: The ability of CAF-1 to preferentially bind to a tetrasome length of DNA (Figure 7a) could ensure sufficient DNA is available so that as histone binding releases the WHD, there will be sufficient space along the DNA for the subsequent assembly of tetrasomes, while simultaneously protecting newly replicated DNA from spurious binding of other factors (Ramachandran and Henikoff, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed model with citation.

claim: Loss of the KER can be compensated by the WHD.
source: Loss of the KER can be compensated by the WHD (Figures 1 and 7b), but deletion of both the KER and WHD renders yeast with a reduced ability to survive DNA damage or maintain gene silencing (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data in Figure 1.

claim: The yKER is shorter than the KER in humans and many other eukaryotes, and correspondingly preferentially recognizes shorter DNA than the hKER in the context of yCAF-1.
source: Moreover, the yKER is shorter than the KER in humans and many other eukaryotes, and correspondingly preferentially recognizes shorter DNA (Figure 6) than the hKER in the context of yCAF-1, which raises the possibility that the KER serves a spacer function to ensure that tetramers are assembled at specific spacings (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data in Figure 6.

claim: The KER SAH acts as a DNA-binding physical spacer element and bridge that links with structural precision multiple functional domains within CAF-1 to configure the architecture of CAF-1 for efficient tetrasome assembly after DNA synthesis.
source: Therefore, we propose that the KER SAH acts as a DNA-binding physical spacer element and bridge that links with structural precision multiple functional domains within CAF-1 to configure the architecture of CAF-1 for efficient tetrasome assembly after DNA synthesis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed model based on all the data presented.
